1024.t: The family house: no electricity, wood stove, tub baths
1024.s: Describes the fourplex house, yard, lamps, plumbing and fetching wood.
1024.q: Yeah, they had, they had a zinc and a, and a, and a faucet and zinc. But we had no bathtub. We had to all take a bath in one of those big, galvanized, number 10 I think, tub.

681.t: Staying with his cabinet-maker uncle and the streetcar to the store
681.s: Hirsch loved staying near the store with a cabinet-maker uncle, rode the streetcar down from Napoleon Avenue; another uncle was an actor.
681.q: No. I used to stay down there with them. I loved it down there because I was, my uncle, who I was very attached to, married to my aunt, my father's sister. And, uh, I loved it down there. I enjoyed it. My uncle was a, was a cabinet maker. And, uh, that's where I think I got my knowledge of cabinet…

298.t: Where he was born and raised in the Irish Channel
298.s: Born on St. Anthony, raised with his uncle on Laura Street after his parents separated.
298.q: What part of town were you brought up in? Up in the 12th Ward. Well I was born on this one. I was raised up in the Irish Channel. Do you know where you were born exactly? On St. Anthony. St. Anthony. Somewhere in the South. I was born in the South. I was born in the South. I was born in the South.

522.t: Mitch Miller's family on Elmira Street
522.s: Mitch Miller's family lived on the street near the grocery store; his mother still lived there.
522.q: Right. Interestingly enough, the street that we lived on is called Martin Street. And a block up from where my father’s grocery store, was a street called Elmira Street. And on Elmira Street was Mitch Miller. And his family lived there. And he of course, by the time

417.t: Born at Magee Hospital; stepfather Thomas Collier and life in Gilmore Alley
417.s: His mother worked at the hospital; stepfather Collier, a Charlie Christian fan, arrives when Benson is seven, and the street cries of Gilmore Alley are described.
417.q: I was born at a place called Magee Hospital. Magee was in a different part of Pittsburgh. It was in – not Schenley. What’s next to Schenley? It’s in Oakland – Oakland, Pittsburgh. My mother ended up working there.

105.t: Pinning down his Central LA neighborhood
105.s: Brown and Hamilton work out where he grew up: south of Central Avenue, east of Watts, toward City Hall, near Lafayette Junior High.
105.q: Compton, you know, Hooper, anything south of Main Street, on the other side of Main Street, which was, you know, down in that area.

116.t: Gert Town, move to Shrewsbury and rural schooling
116.s: Born uptown, the family moves to Jefferson Parish at ten; he describes his sister, the rural school and neighbourhood.
116.q: I was born uptown in a section they call Gert Town. When I was about 10 years old, my father moved the family to Jefferson Parish, because he had bought this property which ultimately became the motel. So I spent from the age of 10 basically until I went in the military. Got out, came back, and…

651.t: Greenhouses, a 1917 tornado and the jazz street names
651.s: Memories of the greenhouses, the chrysanthemum fight, the 1917 tornado, and the streets named for Silver, McLean, Morton and Lake.
651.q: Yes, there were greenhouses. Several of them. Four, I think. Four greenhouses. I want to say four. Five. Yeah. Oh yeah, it was fun when I was a kid. Playing hide-and-go-seek underneath those beds, with the cobwebs and the spiders and stuff, and the chrysanthemums that you could get up in the bed…

111.t: The houses and neighborhood in Pontiac
111.s: He names the three houses he lived in and describes the business-district neighborhood near the church.
111.q: Oh yes! It was 129 Bagley Street. No I’m sorry! The first house, the house I was born in was Orchard Lake. That was the name of the street, Orchard Lake. We moved from there when I was about ten, we moved up into a bigger house up the street from there, about 6 blocks or so. And that was 74 Orchard…

226.s: The family lacked nothing though the house had no electricity or gas, with an outhouse and wood stove.
226.q: In today’s world it would be considered middle class, I would think, because you didn’t want for anything. You had clothing. You had food. You weren’t on any kind of a welfare. There was no – you had all of the things that were – that people had for that time. There was no electricity in that…

614.t: Middle-class Milwaukee neighborhoods of his childhood
614.s: Herman describes his family as middle-class movers who lived in five to eight places in north and northeast Milwaukee.
614.q: From the time I was born, I probably lived in -- oh, at least five or six or seven or eight different locations. But always in the north and northeast part of the city of Milwaukee.
